overall_summary: Space anomalies and mind-bending cosmic phenomena are the primary growth drivers for FACTVERSE, with 'The Planet of Burning Ice' leading at 1,053 views and showing active real-time growth. Conversely, abstract psychology and brain-related topics consistently underperform, struggling to capture initial hook interest and generating minimal engagement.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet of Burning Ice' (1,053 views), 'The Largest Ocean in Space' (460 views), and 'What Does Outer Space Actually Smell Like?' (368 views) represent the channel's top tier of performance.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on extreme space facts that contrast everyday sensory experiences (smell, temperature, state of matter) with cosmic scales.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'Sharks Are Older Than Trees?' (302 views) and 'This Animal Literally Dies Every Winter!' (179 views) outperform standard animal facts.
winning_patterns.action: Frame biological facts around shocking survival mechanisms or historical timeline paradoxes rather than simple trivia.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' (5 and 54 views across duplicate uploads) and 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' (17 views) failed to capture viewer interest.
weak_patterns.action: Avoid introspective or purely educational psychology hooks; if covering the brain, frame it through an external, tangible mystery.

next_video.concept: A planet where it literally snows sunscreen.
next_video.opening_direction: Start with: 'There is a giant planet in our galaxy where it literally snows sunscreen...'
next_video.twist_direction: Reveal that on Kepler-13Ab, it is so hot that titanium dioxide—the active ingredient in sunscreen—gets vaporized into the upper atmosphere and falls back down as snowy precipitation.
next_video.reason: Leverages the highly successful 'extreme cosmic weather/sensory paradox' pattern that drove the channel's best performance ('Burning Ice', 'Glass Rain', 'Diamond Rain') and targets the high-performing midday upload slot.

experiment: Test a 'Time Paradox' style history/science short comparing two unrelated historical events (e.g., 'Woolly Mammoths were still alive when the Pyramids were built') to see if it replicates the success of the 'Sharks older than trees' video.
